Champions' Gala: The Empty Seat
Eight champions. One head table. A ninth chair with no name — just SUPPORT.
At a cross-sport awards gala, eight athletes find a chair labeled SUPPORT and spend the night deciding who gets named, who gets asked, and who gets fries.

The Champions' Gala seats its eight biggest names at a head table with a ninth chair marked only SUPPORT. Before the cameras pan, Jack Whitaker and his tablemates have to ask the people who actually got them here what they want, while Iris drafts a speech Noor never agreed to and Luca learns to stand somewhere other than the center mark. From Jack's side, you decide what the table does with every name, every card, and one invitation to fries.
The gala coordinator with a pen, nine blank place cards, and a run-of-show that's already twelve minutes late.
If nobody asks first, the support crew stays a word on a card, and two private things become somebody else's headline.

The Ninth Chair
Ask the support crew before moving a single card
Ballroom entrance, by the seating chart
Saturday, 6:05 PM
The Grand Lakeshore ballroom smells like lilies and steam-table salmon. On the easel by the doors, the head table has nine chairs. Eight have names.
Chair nine says SUPPORT. That's it. They couldn't even give it a name?
They named the sponsor twice. Once on the chart, once on the napkins. I counted.
I find Table 31 on the chart, wedged against the kitchen doors. Our engineers. Mason's equipment crew. Everyone who actually got us into these suits.
So we drag a mechanic up front to eat salmon on camera. Great. Very respectful.
Or we ask them. Wild concept.
The coordinator hovers with a pen and nine blank place cards. Brody already has one in his hand.
Somebody decided support didn't need a name. I'd like to meet that person. Briefly.
What does the table do about chair nine?
Walk to Table 31 and ask them first.
I cut through forty round tables to the one by the swinging doors. Dana Okoye, our chief race engineer, looks up mid–bread roll.
Gus Pallas, the hockey equipment manager, says no before Jack finishes the question. Dana says maybe — if it's a seat, not a photo op.
Maybe is a name. I'm writing it in pencil.
Jack asked the support crew at Table 31 first; Gus declined, Dana said maybe if it wasn't a photo op, and Brody penciled her name in.
Leave it blank. Ask after they've eaten.
I slide a blank card into the holder. No name, no SUPPORT. Just white.
Blank is worse than SUPPORT. Blank is a ghost.
Blank is a question. Mason, you're asking it after the salads.
Fine. Short questions. I'm good at those.
The table swapped the SUPPORT card for a blank one and agreed Mason would ask the support crew after the salad course.
Don't move anyone. Not for optics.
I'm not parading Dana up here so we look humble on the stream. If anyone from that table wants the chair, they'll say so.
I flip the card over and write ASK US on the back. Small. Facing the table, not the cameras.
Chair nine stays empty. Brody keeps glancing at it like a dog left at the curb.
Jack refused to move anyone for optics; chair nine stayed empty and Brody wrote ASK US on the back of its card.
Center Mark
Take the photo with the engineering crew
The red carpet, hotel entrance
Saturday, 6:40 PM
Twelve feet of red carpet and forty photographers yelling first names. Meridian Racing gets called as a set: Luca and Jack, the golden duo, center mark.
One picture. Then they stop shouting.
I look past him. Our engineers are bunched at the rope line in rented tuxes. Dana is tugging her sleeve. Nobody is calling their names.
They got me here too.
I know.
Then come stand with them.
Center mark. Six years I've stood on it. I don't know what my hands do anywhere else.
A photographer barks Luca's name again. At the rope, Dana catches Jack's eye and gives a tiny headshake: don't make it a thing.
Where does Jack take his picture?
Ask the crew in. Dana only if she agrees.
I ask the crew. Then I ask Dana again, separately. She rolls her eyes and steps in at the edge, exactly where she wanted to be.
Luca walks off the center mark and stands in the second row between two mechanics, grinning like an idiot. It's the best photo of the night.
The flashes haven't faded when Iris Chen shoulders through with a fistful of index cards, Noor two steps behind her like a hostage negotiator.
Emergency. I won Captain of the Year, I get four minutes, and three of them are about Noor. I need witnesses.
Jack asked the crew, and Dana separately, before the photo; Luca left the center mark to stand in the second row with the engineers.
One duo shot for Luca. Then the crew's way.
I get my picture. Three seconds, his shoulder against mine. I'd have taken thirty.
Then I walk to the rope line. The crew takes their own photo on Dana's phone, no press. I'm in it. So is Luca, half out of frame.
Before Jack's back on the carpet, Iris Chen shoulders through with a fistful of index cards, Noor two steps behind like a hostage negotiator.
Emergency. Captain of the Year, four minutes, three of them about Noor. Jack. Congratulations, you're a witness.
Jack gave Luca a three-second duo shot, then joined a press-free crew photo on Dana's phone, with Luca half out of frame.
Skip the carpet. Side door, with the crew.
I duck the rope and walk the crew in through the service entrance, past the ice sculptures. No flashes. Nobody calls anyone's name. It's nice.
I take the picture alone. Center mark, big smile. The photographers love it. I check behind me twice.
In the service hallway, Iris Chen catches Jack by the sleeve, index cards in her other hand. Noor stands two steps behind, arms crossed.
Great, you're avoiding people too. Emergency. I won Captain of the Year, and three of my four minutes are about Noor.
Jack skipped the red carpet and walked the crew in through the service entrance; Luca took his center-mark photo alone.
Card Four
Settle whose permission the speech needs before it's read
Green room, a converted coat check
Saturday, 7:30 PM
The green room used to be a coat check. Iris has six index cards fanned across a folding table. Card four has a small heart in the corner.
Card four's the best one. ‘To the captain across the stage, who makes me better, and who I'm—’
You can be proud of me without telling them who I am to you.
Then I'll talk about your game.
Talk about the semifinal. Talk about my shotcalling. Don't talk about my Tuesdays.
A gala publicist leans in the doorway. “Rival captains, a little spark onstage? The stream would eat it up.”
I'm only here because Iris grabbed me as a witness. Card four is still face-up on the table. Nobody has touched it.
Everyone in this room wants something from that card. Exactly one person gets a vote on it, and she isn't the one holding it.
Whose side does Jack take on card four?
Ask Noor which line she'll let Iris keep.
Noor. Not a vote, not a group thing. Is there a line on that card you'd let her read?
I take the pen. I cross out ‘who I'm—’ and write: ‘who made my year harder and better.’ That's true. That's mine to give.
That's — okay, that's actually better. Don't tell her I said that.
I'm right here.
Noor rewrote one line of card four herself and gave Iris permission to read it; the private part was cut.
Game only. Card four goes to Noor.
Talk about the match. Give card four to the person it's about.
I hand it over. Noor folds it once and tucks it inside her jacket, over her heart, which is a very rude place to put it.
I'll read it later. Alone. That's not a no.
Iris kept her speech to the match; Noor took card four, folded and unread, and said reading it later alone wasn't a no.
Stay out of it. Her speech, her call.
Not my card. Not my speech. I'm going to go find a drink.
The publicist takes Jack's chair. Ten minutes later, card four says ‘someone special across the stage.’ No name. Everyone will know anyway.
Then I'll be across the room. Not across the stage.
She said it calmly. That's the scary version.
Jack stayed out of it; with the publicist's help Iris kept a vague 'someone special across the stage' line, and Noor said she'd sit across the room.
The Cut
Confirm every credit one person at a time — no group yes
Backstage, stage left
Saturday, 8:10 PM
Stage left, ten minutes to Meridian's award. Noor has a pen. She draws one clean line through a private nickname on Iris's card.
This was the best line.
For whom?
For the room.
Tell them about the match.
Mine is worse. Team PR's draft thanks ‘our incredible crew’ and then names exactly two people. Me and Luca.
And put the engineering names back.
Before mine. They earned it.
Fourteen engineers on the roster, ninety seconds of speech. Six seconds a name if nobody coughs. Also, you haven't asked a single one of them.
How does Jack get the names right?
Ask each engineer, one at a time.
Luca and I split the crew between us. One question, fourteen times: how do you want to be named? Not ‘is everyone cool with this.’ Each of them.
Eleven say full names. Rafi wants his nickname. One says no names, please. Dana asks to go last, as ‘race engineer,’ not ‘the heart of the team.’
Nobody said yes for anybody else. That's a first for this team.
Jack and Luca asked all fourteen engineers individually how to be credited; one declined to be named and Dana chose to go last as 'race engineer.'
Thank the crew; name only those who text yes.
I send one message to the crew chat: Reply YES if you want your name read tonight. Silence means no. No means no hard feelings.
Seven yeses before Jack walks on. Dana's comes last: a thumbs-down emoji, then, a minute later, ‘fine. YES.’
Seven names. Forty-two seconds. You'll have time to breathe.
Jack asked the crew to opt in by text; seven engineers, including Dana, said yes to being named, and silence counted as no.
Cut the list. Thank ‘the team’ and walk on.
I'm not reading names I didn't ask about. ‘The team.’ That's what they get tonight, because it's the only thing that's true.
Then I'll ask them after. All fourteen. And I'll put it somewhere that isn't a speech.
Accurate. Also exactly what the sponsor wanted. I hate when those overlap.
Jack refused to read unconfirmed names and thanked only 'the team'; Luca promised to ask all fourteen engineers afterward.
Highlights
Chair nine goes to someone who actually wants it
The main stage
Saturday, 8:45 PM
Hockey's up first. Mason reads the joke on his card about Ethan's glove hand, then crosses it out with the presenter's pen, live, in front of six hundred people.
Short version. We lost Game Seven. I took the penalty.
And I let the goal in. We don't only owe each other the good highlights.
That's annoyingly true.
The room laughs, then goes quiet in the good way. Down at the head table, chair nine is still empty, its card turned toward the stage.
Meridian's next. If anyone's in that chair when the camera pans, it better be because they want to be.
Somebody from Table 31 should get that chair. Nobody from Table 31 should get pushed into it. Those are different sentences.
What happens to chair nine?
Offer Dana the chair and the mic. Her call.
I crouch by Table 31 and say it plainly: the chair's yours, the mic's yours, both optional. Dana looks at the stage for a long time.
She takes the chair. When Meridian is called, she takes the mic for exactly twenty seconds.
“Thank your engineers,” Dana says. “Not tonight. On a Tuesday, when nothing's on fire.” Six hundred people applaud a sentence about Tuesdays.
Dana chose to take chair nine and the mic; she spoke for twenty seconds about thanking engineers on an ordinary Tuesday.
Offer the chair, not the stage.
The chair. No stage, no mic. Dessert's tiramisu. That's the whole offer.
Dana takes chair nine and the tiramisu and declines everything else. When the camera pans, she waves at it with her fork.
Onstage I read her title exactly the way she asked. Then I look down at the head table. She's smiling at her plate.
Dana took chair nine but declined the stage and mic; Jack credited her onstage exactly as she'd asked.
Leave it empty. Put every name on the card.
I write every name from Table 31 on the place card, in pencil, very small. Nineteen of them. Gus Pallas gets the top line because he said no first.
Chair nine stays empty. When the camera pans, the card fills the shot: nineteen names, and nobody forced to sit behind them.
Okay. That's better than a person. Don't tell Dana I said that.
Chair nine stayed empty; Ezra wrote all nineteen Table 31 names on its card, and nobody was made to sit there.
Nobody Wins
Invite him only once you've both finished with your teams
The sidewalk outside the Grand Lakeshore
Saturday, 10:20 PM
Intermission. Valet whistles, wet pavement, the band still audible through the revolving door. Across Lakeshore Drive, a diner sign buzzes: FRIES ALL NIGHT.
Luca is out here with his jacket off and the trophy's ribbon still looped around his wrist. He looks like someone who doesn't know where to stand.
Later. Fries. Across the street. No trophy, no cameras.
Did we win?
It's fries. Nobody wins.
The crew's after-party is at eleven. I promised Dana an hour.
Down the block, Iris hugs every member of Nova goodbye. Across from her, Noor shakes hands with each of Vanta's, in order, like a receiving line.
He didn't say no. He said there's an hour first. Those aren't the same thing, and I'd like to stop confusing them.
How does Jack handle the hour?
Do the crew's hour together. Fries after.
Then we do Dana's hour. Both of us. The fries are open all night. That's the whole point of the sign.
I laugh, which I didn't expect to do out here. I put my jacket back on. We go in together.
Down the block, Noor finishes her receiving line and looks for Iris. Iris is already looking back.
Jack and Luca agreed to spend the crew's hour together first and get fries afterward.
His crew tonight. Fries tomorrow, if he wants.
Go do your hour. Fries tomorrow, noon. Text me yes, or don't. Both are allowed.
You're letting me answer by text? Who are you tonight?
Down the block, Iris and Noor finish their goodbyes and, separately, don't walk toward each other yet.
Jack left Luca's night to his crew and offered fries the next day at noon, answer by text or not at all.
Skip the after-party. Fries at 11:30, his call.
I don't do after-parties. I'll be at that diner at eleven-thirty. You can come or not. Both are fine. One is better.
That's the most honest scheduling I've ever heard.
Luca goes back inside without an answer. Down the block, Iris and Noor each leave the sidewalk with their own teams.
Jack declined the after-party and told Luca he'd be at the diner at 11:30, leaving the choice to him; Luca didn't answer yet.
Trophy on the Table
Keep the invitation separate from the trophy — and the award untouched
The head table, ballroom emptying
Saturday, 11:05 PM
The band packs up. Waiters stack chairs around the head table and leave chair nine alone, like it got promoted.
I hand the Team of the Year trophy to the events manager and ask her to lock it in the hotel safe. It's heavy. It was never mine alone.
You're leaving it?
We're getting fries.
No speech?
You can ask if I want ketchup.
Noor. Tomorrow?
Tomorrow. Tonight is still my team's.
Everyone's asked for one thing at a time tonight, and it worked. I still haven't said what I'm asking Luca for.
What does Jack call the fries?
Say it plainly: it's a date.
It's a date. I'm saying it out loud so you can say no out loud.
I'm not saying no. I'm asking if you want ketchup.
I watch them and decide something. I walk back to Iris and give her a time: ten a.m., coffee, no index cards.
Jack called the fries a date out loud and Luca accepted; Noor then gave Iris a real time for tomorrow: ten a.m. coffee.
Fries as teammates. Ask the rest later.
Fries as teammates tonight. The rest I'll ask when there's no ribbon on your wrist.
Later is allowed. I'm holding you to later.
I don't push Noor for a time. I just say ‘tomorrow’ back, like a password, and let her go.
Jack and Luca kept the fries as teammates, with Jack promising to ask the rest later; Iris let 'tomorrow' stay open.
Teammates only. Say goodnight properly.
I'm going alone. We're teammates, and tonight I want that to be the whole sentence. Thank you for the photo. I mean that.
I nod. I put the ribbon in my pocket. I don't follow him. He was clear, and he was kind about it.
Noor leaves with Vanta. Iris doesn't say ‘tomorrow’ again. Chair nine is the last thing the waiters stack.
Jack told Luca they were teammates only and said a proper goodnight; Noor left with her team and Iris didn't press for tomorrow.
The Empty Seat
Decide how public the night gets — and what happens off the clock
Lou's Diner, across Lakeshore Drive
Sunday, 12:10 AM
Lou's Diner, ten past midnight. Eight people in formalwear wedged into a booth built for six. Chair nine's place card leans against the ketchup.
Ezra's laminating that card. That's not a bit. He brought a sleeve.
Archival. Somebody should keep the record straight.
The door chimes. A gala-stream reporter with a phone on a gimbal spots the booth and lights up like it's Christmas.
“Two minutes! Jack, Luca — the duo shot with the trophy? Iris, card four. Who was it about?”
Short answer: no.
Long answer: their call. Not ours.
All night, every choice was somebody else's to make. This one's partly mine. And it's barely about the reporter.
How does the table end the night?
Answer for yourself. Then tell Luca the truth.
The crew list is on the gala site. Every name on it was asked. Print that. Nothing else at this table is press.
The reporter leaves with Dana's credit and nothing else. Noor slides card four across to Iris: read it to me, then. Just me.
Under the table, I find Luca's hand. I don't make a speech. I ask if he wants ketchup.
Ketchup. And yes, Jack — it's a date. I'm saying it out loud too.
The table gave the reporter only the approved crew credits; Jack and Luca confirmed out loud it was a date, and Noor let Iris read card four to her alone.
Give him chair nine's story. Nothing else.
You want a story? There's a chair with names on it now. Ask us about that.
The reporter gets ten good minutes on support crews and the card Ezra laminated. Nobody asks about Tuesdays.
Luca and I split the fries down the middle, like teammates. Under the table his knee stays against mine. Nobody names that either.
Tomorrow. Tonight is still my team's.
The table gave the reporter only the support-crew story; Jack and Luca stayed teammates for now, and Iris and Noor left 'tomorrow' open.
Give him the duo shot. Leave separately.
I stand, smile, and give the reporter the duo shot — Luca's shoulder, my grin, the picture he wanted at 6:40. For a camera. Not for him.
That was my photo. You just gave it to them.
Iris tells the reporter ‘someone special across the stage,’ and Noor is out the door before the gimbal turns. The trophy stays in the safe. The crew list doesn't change.
Print the crew list. That part was true.
Jack gave the reporter the duo photo instead of giving it to Luca, Iris gave the stream her vague line, and both pairs left separately; the award and crew list stayed unchanged.
Names on Every Card

Ketchup. And yes, Jack — it's a date.

Tomorrow. Tonight is still my team's.
